title: Discriminative Mixture-of-Experts on Graphs
one_liner: When graph models split their work across multiple expert sub-networks, teaching them which nodes go to which expert leads to a better split, and weighing their answers by confidence fixes the uncertain guesses.
lead: Graph neural networks scale by splitting their work across many expert sub-networks — each expert becomes good at finding a different kind of pattern in the graph. But when you leave the routing (which expert gets which node) loose, experts become identical copies and the router picks the same few experts for everything. This paper fixes both by explicitly teaching the router to separate nodes into groups with similar properties and by down-weighting answers from experts who express doubt.

problem.h2: Experts become clones and routes collapse
paras: A graph is a web of nodes (like people) connected by edges (like friendships). A graph neural network reads that web and predicts something about each node. To handle huge graphs, researchers split the network into multiple expert sub-networks, because one large network becomes slow to train and run. Each expert is smaller, so each can be trained faster. If you give each expert a different slice of nodes, each expert can learn just the patterns in its slice. Some experts get better at finding local clusters (nodes close together look alike), others at spotting bridges between clusters (long edges connecting far parts), others at detecting loops. Different graph patterns need different experts because a single network cannot specialize in all patterns at once — there is a trade-off between being good at everything and being excellent at one thing.

The naive approach: send each node to one expert, randomly or via a simple score. The problem is that without feedback, all experts start learning the same patterns. They become clones. At the same time, the router (the part that decides which expert gets which node) starts favoring the same few experts — it routes 90 percent of nodes to expert 1 and ignores experts 2 and 3. This collapse wastes the capacity you paid for. Diverse patterns go unrecognized.

callout.html: The paper uses contrastive learning to force the router to group nodes by semantic similarity, and reweights expert answers by confidence.

steps.text: Identify which nodes are semantically similar (nodes that should go to the same expert).
Add a training signal that pushes nodes in the same cluster toward the same expert and pulls nodes from different clusters apart.
Ensure no expert gets overloaded by too many nodes, distributing work fairly.
Each expert processes its assigned nodes and predicts their properties.
Down-weight experts that express uncertainty, up-weight those expressing confident predictions.

paras: The paper changes two things: the routing signal (how decisions are guided during training) and the fusion weights (how much each expert answer counts in the final prediction).

hidden.h2: Routing confidence: how sure is the router?
hidden.name: routing confidence
paras: As the router assigns nodes to experts, it outputs a confidence score for each assignment (how much the network believes this node belongs to this expert). A score near 1 means the router is certain; a score near 0.5 means the router is confused.

The paper measures routing confidence by looking at the scores the router assigns across all nodes, then computing the average. Low average confidence means the router is uncertain about most assignments — a red flag. High confidence means the router has clear opinions. The paper shows that this confidence strongly predicts whether the model will work well: confident routers lead to good answers, uncertain routers fail.

heat.caption: Darker means the router is more confident in that node-to-expert assignment. Nodes routed with high confidence (dark) get expert answers that count more.

reads.html: When a router assigns a node to an expert, it can be certain or unsure. Certain assignments (the node clearly belongs here) get high confidence; unsure assignments (could go either way) get low confidence. The paper measures this by looking at how spread out the router's choice is across experts: if it picks one expert and ignores the others, that is high confidence; if it gives similar probability to many experts, that is low confidence. Then the paper gives more weight to answers from high-confidence experts.

The paper defines routing confidence as how peaky the router's score distribution is. If the router outputs (0.9, 0.05, 0.05) across three experts, that is high confidence. If it outputs (0.35, 0.35, 0.3), that is low confidence. The paper tests this on real graphs and finds that nodes with low routing confidence lead to poor final predictions. Theoretically, the error bounds show that this confidence directly predicts how well the model generalizes.

mechanism.h2: The causal chain: why changing routing and weighting works
paras: The mechanism has two parts. First, contrastive routing: the paper adds a training loss that says 'if two nodes are semantically similar (they should behave the same way), then send them to the same expert.' This is like telling the router: 'You will be penalized for splitting up nodes that look alike.' As training progresses, the router learns to cluster semantically similar nodes. When nodes of the same type all go to the same expert, that expert specializes — it sees many examples of one pattern and learns it well. At the same time, different experts get different types of nodes, so they diverge instead of converging to clones.

Second, confidence-aware fusion: after each expert answers, the paper computes a confidence score for that expert's prediction on that node (e.g., how peaky is the output distribution — is the expert saying one answer loudly or hedging?). Answers with high confidence (the expert is certain) get multiplied by a weight close to 1; answers with low confidence (the expert is unsure) get multiplied by a weight close to 0. This down-weights the garbage guesses. Because the router's uncertainty in step 1 correlates with bad answers, low-confidence experts are often the ones with uncertain nodes, so this reweighting removes noise from the final prediction.

Together: forced semantic clustering makes experts specialize, and confidence reweighting removes guesses the model doesn't trust. Both target the same failure — homogenized experts and collapsed routing — from different angles.

stages.s: Nodes and their neighborhoods in the graph
Router scores nodes and assigns them to experts (with contrastive guidance on semantic similarity)
Each expert processes its assigned nodes in parallel
Experts output predictions and confidence scores
Reweight expert answers by their confidence

math.h2: The equation: contrastive routing loss and confidence fusion
math.words: The training loss combines three parts: the main prediction loss (how wrong the guesses are), a contrastive routing term (pull nodes of the same semantic cluster toward the same expert), and a load-balance term (keep expert assignments balanced). When making the final answer, reweight each expert's output by its confidence score.
math.equation:
Loss_total = Loss_pred + lambda_c * Loss_contrastive + lambda_lb * Loss_load_balance
Final_answer = sum_e ( confidence_e * expert_e(node) )
symbols: prediction loss; how wrong the model's guesses are
penalty for splitting semantically similar nodes across different experts
how strongly to enforce semantic clustering in routing
how much to penalize imbalanced expert load
penalty for overloading one expert and starving others
how confident expert e is in its prediction (ranges 0 to 1)
the prediction from expert e for this node

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose nodes 1 and 2 are in the same semantic cluster. Naive routing sends node 1 to expert A and node 2 to expert B. Contrastive loss penalizes this split (they should go to the same place), say +5 to Loss_contrastive.
Paper's routing sends both to expert A. Now Loss_contrastive = 0 (they went the same place, good).
Expert A outputs prediction 0.8 with high confidence (confidence_A = 0.9). Expert B predicts 0.2 with low confidence (confidence_B = 0.3).
Naive fusion: (0.8 + 0.2) / 2 = 0.5 (confused answer, splitting the difference).
Confidence fusion: 0.9 * 0.8 + 0.3 * 0.2 = 0.72 + 0.06 = 0.78 (weighted toward the confident expert, much cleaner).

math.note: The contrastive loss guides the router to cluster nodes by meaning, and the confidence reweighting removes noise from uncertain experts, together blocking expert collapse and unstable routing.

bars.h2: Performance: naive routing vs. contrastive routing with confidence fusion

charts.title: Naive graph-MoE
charts.note: Experts collapse to one; the router is confused; accuracy suffers because most nodes go to the same expert, which is now a generalist instead of a specialist.

charts.title: C2GMoE (this paper)
charts.note: Contrastive routing spreads nodes across experts by semantic meaning; experts specialize; confidence weighting removes uncertain predictions; routing is stable and all experts are active.

items.html: If the weight lambda_c is too small, the contrastive signal does not override the main loss, and routing still collapses. The paper needs to tune this weight per dataset.
Contrastive routing requires knowing which nodes are semantically similar. If the graph has no clear clusters or the method to find them is noisy, contrastive guidance misleads the router.

If experts assign high confidence to wrong answers (they are certain but wrong), reweighting actually amplifies the error. The paper assumes confidence correlates with correctness, which can break on noisy data.

items.b: Load imbalance grows despite load-balance loss.
items.html: If one semantic cluster is much larger than others, the load-balance term cannot force an even split without violating the contrastive constraint. The method has to trade off between semantic correctness and balanced load.

With careful tuning of lambda_c and lambda_lb, semantic clusters that match the data's true structure, and confidence scores that reflect actual prediction quality, the method specializes experts and stabilizes routing.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a graph classification task (e.g., node classification on a standard dataset like Cora or OGB). Compare three setups: (1) a naive graph-MoE with random or uniform routing, (2) the same MoE with only contrastive routing (no confidence reweighting), and (3) the full C2GMoE with both contrastive routing and confidence-aware fusion. Track three metrics across training: (a) how many distinct experts are actively used (should be close to the number of experts for C2GMoE, much lower for naive), (b) the average routing confidence score (should be higher for C2GMoE, indicating the router is certain), and (c) node classification accuracy on a held-out test set (should be highest for C2GMoE). Plot all three over epochs. The demo must make impossible to miss that contrastive routing alone raises utilization and confidence, and adding confidence fusion pushes accuracy higher.
demo.metric_eq:
Specialization = (number of experts with >5 percent of nodes assigned) / (total experts)
Routing_confidence = mean(max-softmax of router scores across all nodes)
Accuracy = (correct predictions) / (total nodes)
demo.closing: The demo should show three lines on one plot: naive (all metrics low), contrastive-only (utilization and confidence rise), and full method (all three metrics peak). This proves the two pieces — routing semantics and confidence reweighting — both matter.
